fieldGuide.camo.overview: Paint helps concealment when its region matches the battlefield. Staying hidden also depends on movement, foliage and firing.
fieldGuide.camo.0.title: Match the terrain
fieldGuide.camo.0.body: Auto chooses a matching seasonal pattern. A compatible manual pattern adds 3.5 percentage points to your own camouflage before firing penalties. Factory restores the stock appearance; choosing a country collection alone does not grant the bonus.
fieldGuide.camo.1.title: Put foliage on the sightline
fieldGuide.camo.1.body: Bushes conceal a tank only when they cross the enemy’s sightline. Solid terrain and buildings can block that line entirely. A green paint job in the open is not a substitute for cover.
fieldGuide.camo.2.title: Concealment is not cover
fieldGuide.camo.2.body: A ridge or solid building blocks a sightline that actually intersects it. Foliage instead contributes concealment along that line; it does not stop shells. Firing reduces your camouflage and removes nearby foliage benefits within 15 m, while more distant foliage can still help. The marked lines illustrate these distinctions, not a live visibility test.
fieldGuide.maps.overview: Read a battlefield as routes, sightlines and protected positions—not just a backdrop.
fieldGuide.maps.0.title: Choose a route
fieldGuide.maps.0.body: Open lanes favor long sightlines. Buildings, rocks and ridges divide the map into shorter engagements. Pick a route that gives your vehicle room to turn and a covered retreat.
fieldGuide.maps.1.title: Work the ridge
fieldGuide.maps.1.body: A ridge can hide your hull while you expose the gun. Your gun’s depression limit determines whether you can aim downhill without driving farther over the crest.
fieldGuide.maps.2.title: Cross exposed ground
fieldGuide.maps.2.body: The village crossroads joins several firing lanes. Check the exits before crossing, use buildings to break sightlines, and avoid stopping in the intersection. Terrain, slopes and water change traction; a route that looks short may still be slow.
fieldGuide.dossier.overview: Use the dossier to connect a vehicle’s numbers with its battlefield role.
fieldGuide.dossier.0.title: Compare like with like
fieldGuide.dossier.0.body: Start with role and tier, then compare mobility, protection and firepower. A high summary rating is a comparison aid, not a promise that the vehicle wins every duel.
fieldGuide.dossier.1.title: Read the actual values
fieldGuide.dossier.1.body: Check gun limits, ammunition, reload behavior and nominal armor. Garage bars compare peers; equipped bonuses appear alongside stock values so you can see what your loadout changes.
fieldGuide.dossier.2.title: Inspect the layout
fieldGuide.dossier.2.body: Open the Gallery’s armor, module and crew layers to see where combat volumes sit. These diagrams describe the game’s authored combat model, not real-world engineering measurements.
fieldGuide.performance.overview: Speed, turning, vision and survivability describe different strengths. Build a plan around the combination.
fieldGuide.performance.0.title: Acceleration matters
fieldGuide.performance.0.body: Top speed is a limit, not a speed you reach instantly. Vehicle power, ground resistance and slope affect how quickly you move between positions.
fieldGuide.performance.1.title: Keep a way out
fieldGuide.performance.1.body: Turning and reverse speed matter when withdrawing behind cover. Avoid exposing your side just to turn around after taking a shot.
fieldGuide.performance.2.title: Read visibility separately
fieldGuide.performance.2.body: View range helps you detect enemies; camouflage makes your own vehicle harder to detect. Neither ignores solid cover. Equipment-adjusted values describe your selected loadout.
fieldGuide.protection.overview: A hit is resolved against the plate it strikes. Nominal thickness is only the starting point.
fieldGuide.protection.0.title: Find the impact plate
fieldGuide.protection.0.body: Hull and turret fronts, sides and rears have different protection. A frontal armor number does not apply to the whole silhouette. Use the armor layer to inspect the actual layout.
fieldGuide.protection.1.title: Consider the angle
fieldGuide.protection.1.body: An oblique shot travels through a longer path of armor. Shell normalization, ricochet and overmatch rules also matter, so an angle alone cannot predict the result.
fieldGuide.protection.2.title: Protect weak areas
fieldGuide.protection.2.body: Angle with care: turning too far may expose a thinner side plate. Use terrain to hide vulnerable areas and recheck which plate the enemy can actually hit.
fieldGuide.ammunition.overview: Pick a shell for the target and the shot you can actually make. Penetration and damage answer different questions.
fieldGuide.ammunition.0.title: Compare penetration
fieldGuide.ammunition.0.body: The ammunition card shows penetration at close range and at 1 km where applicable. Compare the selected shell with the plate and angle you expect to hit, not just the enemy’s vehicle name.
fieldGuide.ammunition.1.title: Understand the impact
fieldGuide.ammunition.1.body: AP-family, shaped-charge and explosive rounds resolve impacts differently. Damage is not guaranteed by the listed penetration value; a bounce, failed penetration or external hit can produce a different result.
fieldGuide.ammunition.2.title: Watch the firing cycle
fieldGuide.ammunition.2.body: A ready round, a magazine reload and a missile channel are different states. Follow the active weapon’s readiness indicator rather than assuming every ammunition choice shares one reload.
fieldGuide.armament.overview: Hull direction, turret rotation and gun elevation are separate parts of aiming.
fieldGuide.armament.0.title: Turn the turret
fieldGuide.armament.0.body: The turret follows the aim direction within the vehicle’s traversal limits. A target outside the current gun direction cannot be hit just because the camera can see it.
fieldGuide.armament.1.title: Use depression
fieldGuide.armament.1.body: The barrel has a minimum and maximum vertical angle. At a crest, insufficient depression can leave the gun above a nearby target even when the target is visible.
fieldGuide.armament.2.title: Move the hull
fieldGuide.armament.2.body: Reposition the tank when terrain or articulation limits block the shot. In the Gallery, change hull, turret and gun controls independently to understand the available firing arc.
fieldGuide.modules.overview: An impact can damage a system inside the tank as well as reduce vehicle health.
fieldGuide.modules.0.title: Follow the hit path
fieldGuide.modules.0.body: Internal damage depends on which modeled volumes the damaging path reaches. The module layer shows their locations; a visible equipment detail is not automatically a damageable module.
fieldGuide.modules.1.title: Notice the consequence
fieldGuide.modules.1.body: Engine, tracks, gun and ammunition storage serve different functions. Read the damaged-system indicator to understand why movement or firing behavior has changed.
fieldGuide.modules.2.title: Protect the layout
fieldGuide.modules.2.body: Avoid repeatedly exposing the same vulnerable side. Inspect the selected vehicle’s actual module diagram rather than assuming every tank places its engine and ammunition in the same location.
fieldGuide.crew.overview: Crew stations are modeled separately from the mechanical modules they operate.
fieldGuide.crew.0.title: Locate the stations
fieldGuide.crew.0.body: This in-game X-ray shows the Abrams commander and gunner inside the turret. The colored figures mark internal stations, not passengers sitting on the roof. Open the selected-vehicle diagrams below for your tank’s own arrangement.
fieldGuide.crew.1.title: Read the role
fieldGuide.crew.1.body: The blue driver station sits forward in this Abrams hull. Driver, gunner, loader and commander have different jobs; turret stations rotate with the turret while hull stations stay with the hull.
fieldGuide.crew.2.title: Respond to casualties
fieldGuide.crew.2.body: The pink loader illustrates a separate crew station; vehicles with other loading systems may have a different crew. Injuries and mechanical damage are separate states. Check the affected role and available consumables before deciding whether to withdraw.
fieldGuide.equipment.overview: Three equipment slots tune a vehicle for your preferred role.
fieldGuide.equipment.0.title: Tune the weapon
fieldGuide.equipment.0.body: Use your three equipment slots to support a role. Weapon equipment can change reload, aiming or dispersion where eligible. These are gameplay modifiers; fitting an item does not necessarily add visible hardware to the model.
fieldGuide.equipment.1.title: Match the vehicle
fieldGuide.equipment.1.body: Mobility equipment helps a vehicle reach and leave positions. Availability depends on class and weapon system, and the loadout is saved per vehicle. Choose from the items offered for your selected tank.
fieldGuide.equipment.2.title: Read the improved values
fieldGuide.equipment.2.body: The stats already show your equipment-adjusted values, including rotation, dispersion and observation where affected. Conditional equipment still needs its activation conditions; stationary observation and concealment bonuses are not always active.
fieldGuide.special.overview: Use the fitted vehicle controls independently of the main gun. The labels below show default keyboard bindings; the live HUD reflects your own bindings.
fieldGuide.special.0.title: Launch smoke
fieldGuide.special.0.body: On equipped vehicles, the Smoke control launches the turret-mounted canisters. The default key is G. Open the Smoke entry for the real launch arcs, screen behavior and charge limits.
fieldGuide.special.1.title: Use the roof gun
fieldGuide.special.1.body: The default B key toggles a supported automatic roof weapon. It needs a spotted opponent, a clear firing lane and a target within its aiming limits and range. It is independent of the main gun; not every visible machine gun is an automatic system.
fieldGuide.special.2.title: Lights and special actions
fieldGuide.special.2.body: N toggles the fitted lights by default. Other controls appear only when applicable: ATGM selection, suspension and Gravity Mode jump each follow their own rules. Use the live control strip for remapped keys, touch controls, charges and cooldowns.
fieldGuide.layers.overview: Each inspection layer answers a different question about the same vehicle.
fieldGuide.layers.0.title: Appearance and armor
fieldGuide.layers.0.body: Appearance shows the rendered vehicle. Armor shows authored protection plates. A decorative mesh and a combat plate are different things; use the appropriate layer for your question.
fieldGuide.layers.1.title: Modules and crew
fieldGuide.layers.1.body: Internal overlays reveal system and crew volumes. Rotate the vehicle and turret to understand their placement and ownership rather than judging depth from one side view.
fieldGuide.layers.2.title: Surface markup
fieldGuide.layers.2.body: Markup selects visible surfaces for review. It records annotations and screenshots without changing vehicle balance, armor thickness or the playable model.
fieldGuide.markup.overview: Mark the exact surface you mean, then export enough context for another person to find it.
fieldGuide.markup.0.title: Pick a surface
fieldGuide.markup.0.body: Choose face or patch scope before selecting the visible mesh. The selection follows its owning hull or turret as you change the pose.
fieldGuide.markup.1.title: Add context
fieldGuide.markup.1.body: Use the inspection readout and annotations to explain the issue. Keep the camera close enough to identify the surface, with enough surrounding geometry to show its location.
fieldGuide.markup.2.title: Export the review
fieldGuide.markup.2.body: Save the JSON and PNG together when sharing a review. The JSON preserves the selection record; the image shows what you were looking at. Neither edits the playable tank.
fieldGuide.camera.overview: Position and framing are separate choices. Set the view to explain the subject before capturing it.
fieldGuide.camera.0.title: Choose the viewpoint
fieldGuide.camera.0.body: A side view explains length and gun placement; a top view explains layout; a three-quarter view shows overall form. Choose the angle that answers the question.
fieldGuide.camera.1.title: Frame the subject
fieldGuide.camera.1.body: Keep the important parts inside the frame, including a long barrel or the direction of motion. Moving the camera and changing field of view produce different perspective relationships.
fieldGuide.camera.2.title: Keep a repeatable view
fieldGuide.camera.2.body: Use Gallery view presets for consistent inspection. In Studio, save the camera transform in a shot or recipe so the same composition can be restored later.
fieldGuide.environment.overview: Set the battlefield first: its seed, lighting and weather establish the scene your actors will occupy.
fieldGuide.environment.0.title: Choose the world
fieldGuide.environment.0.body: Select a battlefield and seed before placing actors. A saved recipe keeps this context together so later work starts from the same intended scene.
fieldGuide.environment.1.title: Set the light
fieldGuide.environment.1.body: Day, sunset and night change the lighting mood. Check silhouettes and important surfaces after changing time of day; a pose readable at noon may disappear in shadow.
fieldGuide.environment.2.title: Review the background
fieldGuide.environment.2.body: Weather, terrain and surrounding objects should support the subject. Check the final camera view before adding effects, then keep the environment in the exported recipe.
fieldGuide.actors.overview: Studio actors are staged vehicles. Give each one a clear position, pose and purpose in the shot.
fieldGuide.actors.0.title: Add a vehicle
fieldGuide.actors.0.body: Choose a first-party vehicle from the roster. Each added actor is a separate instance, so two copies of the same model can occupy different positions and play different roles.
fieldGuide.actors.1.title: Stage the pose
fieldGuide.actors.1.body: Select the actor before changing position, hull direction, turret direction or gun elevation. These controls act on different parts of the rig; check the gun’s direction in the camera view.
fieldGuide.actors.2.title: Keep identity clear
fieldGuide.actors.2.body: Paint and staged damage help tell the story. When building motion or effect tracks, verify which actor is selected so a shot or movement is attached to the intended vehicle.
fieldGuide.effects.overview: Effects are timed events. Place the cause and the result on the same scene clock.
fieldGuide.effects.0.title: Choose the source
fieldGuide.effects.0.body: Attach a firing event to the intended actor, or place an impact at the intended terrain location. A beautiful explosion in the wrong place makes the sequence harder to understand.
fieldGuide.effects.1.title: Set the timing
fieldGuide.effects.1.body: Place firing, impact and destruction events at their intended times. Scrub around the event to check the relationship between the muzzle, target and camera.
fieldGuide.effects.2.title: Check the final frame
fieldGuide.effects.2.body: Smoke and debris can obscure the subject. Review the actual capture time and camera, then save the recipe so actor poses and event times stay together.
fieldGuide.timeline.overview: Camera keys, actor tracks and effects share one timeline. Their timing creates the sequence.
fieldGuide.timeline.0.title: Place key moments
fieldGuide.timeline.0.body: Set the opening composition, the action and the ending. Camera keys store viewpoints; actor tracks store vehicle motion. They are separate tracks on the same clock.
fieldGuide.timeline.1.title: Choose the transition
fieldGuide.timeline.1.body: A cut holds the previous view until the next key. Interpolated transitions travel between keys. Inspect the path between keyframes, not only the endpoints.
fieldGuide.timeline.2.title: Scrub and replay
fieldGuide.timeline.2.body: Move the playhead through the whole shot to check actor motion and event timing. A still frame freezes one moment; a video also reveals awkward transitions and late effects.
fieldGuide.output.overview: A capture is the image or video. A recipe is the scene data needed to rebuild the setup. Keep both.
fieldGuide.output.0.title: Compose the frame
fieldGuide.output.0.body: Check the camera, playhead and selected output settings. Important action should remain readable at the final crop, not just in the editing workspace.
fieldGuide.output.1.title: Capture the result
fieldGuide.output.1.body: Use a still for a single moment and video for movement over time. Review the exported file for framing and timing before using it in promotional material.
fieldGuide.output.2.title: Save the recipe
fieldGuide.output.2.body: Export the scene JSON alongside the media. It preserves the setup for another capture or edit; the image alone cannot restore actors, camera keys and event timing.
fieldGuide.recipe.overview: Recreate the setup behind a frame, then adapt it to your own shot.
fieldGuide.recipe.0.title: Copy the scene
fieldGuide.recipe.0.body: Copy the recipe with the button below. The data records scene settings such as map, actors, camera and timeline; a preview image only shows the intended result.
fieldGuide.recipe.1.title: Load in Studio
fieldGuide.recipe.1.body: Open Scene Studio and use its JSON load controls to restore the recipe. Loading a recipe changes the current scene, so save work you want to keep first.
fieldGuide.recipe.2.title: Review and adapt
fieldGuide.recipe.2.body: Check the camera and playhead after loading, then adjust the shot and capture again. Recipes preserve scene intent; later renderer or asset changes can alter the resulting pixels.

docs.guide.vehicles.1.t: Choose a role, then a vehicle
docs.guide.vehicles.1.p1: Light tanks and reconnaissance IFVs trade protection for scouting, repositioning and support. The Sheridan family leads the fleet in base view range. A high view range does not reveal every enemy: camouflage, cover, smoke and line of sight still determine detection. Main battle tanks combine armor, gun handling and mobility in different proportions; a heavy front plate does not protect the sides, roof or internal modules.
docs.guide.vehicles.1.p2: Use the searchable fleet reference below to compare base hull and turret rotation, dispersion, aim time, reload, speed, view range and supported systems. These are game balance values, not claims about classified real-world performance. Garage figures include your fitted equipment; mode bonuses and combat damage can change the resulting battle performance.
docs.guide.vehicles.2.p1: The compact console above ammunition only offers systems that the selected vehicle or mode supports. E selects or toggles an ATGM, G launches smoke, N toggles lights, B toggles a remote automatic gun, and F jumps in jump-enabled modes. The displayed key hints are the immediate reference. A reload countdown replaces the weapon label while that system is unavailable.
docs.guide.vehicles.2.p2: Smoke grenades leave the authored launcher sockets, fly forward in an arc and develop into expanding, drifting clouds. They interrupt spotting and targeting through the cloud, providing space to withdraw or cross an exposed lane. Smoke does not stop shells already in flight. Remote guns need a suitable visible target and a clear firing path; they animate independently of the main cannon. Hydropneumatic aiming is only available on vehicles equipped for it.
docs.guide.vehicles.3.p1: Equipment benefits appear directly in the final garage values rather than as an old-to-new comparison. Compare turret traverse and dispersion as well as reload, mobility and vision: a handling improvement can matter more than raw damage. Each shell has its own penetration, velocity, damage and ammunition count. Guided racks and conventional cannon ammunition may use different reload channels.
docs.guide.vehicles.3.p2: Open the information controls or Tank Gallery for vehicle-specific armor, module and crew diagrams generated from the actual first-party model. They explain why a hit can disable a track, damage an engine or injure crew without destroying the hull. The current vehicle geometry and calibration receipts, rather than one generic tank drawing, supply these diagrams.
docs.guide.simulation.1.p1: Regular Battle is elimination: defeat the opposing team before the fifteen-minute clock ends. Destroyed vehicles do not respawn. The scoreboard carries the essential information, so this mode has no extra objective banner. Choose 7 v 7, 14 v 14 or custom teams before launch. In custom solo battles, the player counts as an ally; the field limit is 42 vehicles and allied bots yield when needed to preserve the requested enemy count.
docs.guide.simulation.1.p2: Battle Setup stores settings for each mode. Team presets, enemy nation and eligible times of day are chosen before starting. The Battle button launches the configured game; Multiplayer has its own entry for creating or joining a room without accidentally starting a solo match.
docs.guide.simulation.2.p1: Take the enemy flag back to your own base while protecting your home flag. The default target is three captures, with a fifteen-minute clock and six-second respawns; setup can change the score and respawn settings. Carrying a flag reduces speed to 85% of normal. Recovering a dropped friendly flag and escorting a carrier can be more valuable than chasing a distant kill.
docs.guide.simulation.2.p2: Use fast vehicles for the run, keep a defender near home and cover the carrier’s return lane. Bots assign carrier, recovery, escort, raid and defense roles rather than sending the entire team to one flag. Destroying an enemy opens a route, but a kill is not a flag capture.
docs.guide.simulation.3.p1: Zone Control rewards taking and holding three sectors. The default target is 750 points, with six-second respawns and a fifteen-minute clock. Destroying an opposing tank adds 25 points in Zone Control and Gravity Mode. Spread pressure across the map: leaving every sector to pursue one damaged tank gives the enemy time to score.
docs.guide.simulation.3.p2: Gravity Mode uses the zone objective with a twelve-minute clock, rocket jumps, boosted mobility and selectable gravity. Mars is 0.38 g, Moon 0.17 g and Earth 1 g. Cache frequency is configurable. Its default vehicle modifiers are 1.25× speed, 1.2× hull health, 0.9× damage and 0.9× reload time. Recoil and airborne motion matter: choose a landing zone before launching.
docs.guide.simulation.4.p1: Drive or shoot the ball into the enemy goal. The default match lasts ten minutes, ends at five goals and uses three-second respawns. Vehicles have 0.6 g gravity, 1.85× speed, 1.5× hull health, half damage and 0.7× reload time. Ammunition is unlimited; equipment, consumables and critical module damage are disabled for this mode.
docs.guide.simulation.4.p2: Get behind the ball, line up the goal and commit to a controlled push. Jumping and amplified recoil enable aerial plays but can overshoot the ball. A striker, supporting screens and a goal defender make a stronger team than several tanks wedged around the same contact point. Destroying tanks disrupts the opposition; goals decide the score.
docs.guide.simulation.5.p1: Endless Horde has no match clock or respawns. Survive waves that grow from five attackers by one each wave, with an additional surge every third wave under the default settings. Clearing a wave repairs 30% of maximum hull health; use the floating repair and ammunition caches to sustain the run. Setup can change the allied support, hostile identity pool, opening wave and enemy nation.
docs.guide.simulation.5.p2: Frontline Assault is a sequential breakthrough: take three sectors against escalating defenders, then hold the final sector for twenty seconds. The default clock is twelve minutes and running out of time is a defeat. Campaign operations vary the battlefield and difficulty; clearing an operation opens the next. Preserve your hull for the final hold rather than treating it like a respawn mode.
docs.guide.simulation.6.p1: Movement runs at a fixed sixty steps per second. Engine power, weight, forward and reverse limits, track condition, terrain resistance and hull rotation jointly determine handling. The renderer interpolates those states rather than changing movement with frame rate. Handbrake behavior is grounded; landing after a jump must not silently latch the brake.
docs.guide.simulation.6.p2: A fall is a physical impact, not just a height threshold. Mass, impact speed, attitude and mode physics affect the result. Reduced gravity changes both your arc and the terrain you can safely reach. Avoid blind drops at bridge abutments or cliff edges; use a route with a visible landing and enough room to settle.
docs.guide.worlds.1.t: Picking maps and times of day
docs.guide.worlds.1.p1: The current catalog contains 33 battlefields. Pick a specific map or use Random. Ordinary random selection excludes the dedicated Mars and Moon battlefields, and consecutive solo draws avoid the previous map. Multiplayer uses the host’s selected battlefield so every peer shares the same world. The full atlas below uses the approved current map pictures.
docs.guide.worlds.1.p2: Day, sunset and night are weighted 60:30:10 when all are enabled. Disabling a time redistributes those weights over the remaining choices; at least one must remain enabled. Earthrise Basin places a large Earth in its lunar sky. Aegis Crossing is a lush green cliff-and-bridge battlefield with buildings around the crossing. Read routes and elevation as well as the thumbnail: a spectacular drop can still be fatal.
docs.guide.interface.1.t: A compact garage and readable battle HUD
docs.guide.interface.1.p1: Open Choose how you play to configure each mode, then use Battle to launch. The separate hexagonal Multiplayer control opens room setup. Map cards show compact biome tags; hover reveals the magnifier, and selecting an already selected map opens its larger preview. Camouflage names occupy one line, with compact collection and nation filters above the scrollable swatches.
docs.guide.interface.1.p2: Hold Tab to expand the team lists. Lists remain readable through 14 vehicles per side; larger teams use an icon grid. The penetration panel simplifies its numeric detail for large rosters so the vehicle diagrams remain contained and visible. Scope magnification sits with the central aiming information. Objective, detection and team notifications occupy separate reserved areas; Regular Battle omits the extra objective strip.
docs.guide.interface.2.t: Settings, clean captures and phone orientation
docs.guide.interface.2.p1: Settings separates gameplay, sound, graphics and language. Choose AI difficulty and Classic or Jev behavior for the next battle. The UI-free setting hides gameplay overlays for unobstructed viewing; restore it through Settings when you need the HUD again. It is a viewing control, not a replay export or an automatic promotion workflow.
docs.guide.interface.2.p2: On phones, test both portrait and landscape, including rotation while a menu is open. Short landscape drawers reserve actual space for map cards and camouflage swatches; detection and countdowns must leave touch controls usable. Automated layout checks cover 568×320, 667×375, 844×390, 932×430 and a 844×300 browser-chrome case, plus Chinese text. These checks supplement physical-device testing; they do not establish performance on every phone.
docs.guide.ai.1.p1: Classic and Jev share the local driving, aiming, visibility and vehicle-system logic on both allied and enemy teams. Jev adds bounded team-level orders; it does not bypass spotting or replace the physical driver. Choose the brain and difficulty before the next match. An allied team should not retain an older behavior set just because it fights alongside the player.
docs.guide.ai.1.p2: Flag teams distribute recovery, escort and raiding roles. Turbo Ball retains a striker long enough to circle behind the ball and line up a push, with screening and defensive support. Zone teams distribute capture pressure. Mobile units can flank while anchors maintain pressure; navigation includes right-of-way for the human, committed passing and safe reversing when vehicles block one another.
docs.guide.ai.2.t: Smoke, remote guns and safe jumps
docs.guide.ai.2.p1: Bots can deploy fitted smoke when withdrawing, under pressure or reloading, and operate remote automatic guns against eligible visible opponents. They only request a jump when the mode allows it and the prospective landing is affordable. Cliff and bridge approaches need a valid route; a direct line to the objective is not enough.
docs.guide.ai.2.p2: Behavior tests include all 33 maps, flag and ball scenarios, congestion, fall-risk decisions and a large Jev team workload. Their guarantees are scoped to the tested scenarios: they catch regressions in decisions and bounded work, but do not prove that a bot will solve every possible terrain or traffic situation.
docs.guide.rendering.1.p1: Driving lights use actual model apertures and follow the hull’s pose. Their warm beams now illuminate farther ahead; only the nearest eligible sources occupy a fixed light pool, while the other visible lamp lenses may still glow. Switching lights off or destroying a tank removes its contribution. Periscopes, mirrors and unrelated armor must not glow just because they share a material.
docs.guide.rendering.1.p2: Ambient occlusion and cast shadows are separate. Turning AO off should not remove sun shadows. Shadow stability, cloud history and effects composition have dedicated checks for moving cameras, firing and quality changes. Smoke is both a rendered volume effect and a simulation visibility blocker; the picture and the spotting decision have separate owners that must agree.
docs.guide.performance.1.p1: The browser may reclaim a graphics context under memory pressure. The game pauses presentation and restores resources behind cover before resuming. Quality recovery should be bounded, preserve the battle state and avoid repeated allocation. A reload is the fallback when restoration cannot complete; it is not the normal way to switch maps or vehicles.
docs.guide.performance.1.p2: When a regular tab behaves differently from a fresh tab, compare the served application version and saved graphics settings before attributing it to one render effect. Hashed assets and deployment-version checks protect against mixed releases. Record the map, vehicle, quality, viewport and reproduction steps with a report; a screenshot alone cannot establish whether the cause is stale assets, settings or GPU state.
docs.guide.studio.1.p1: Public screenshots and videos are curated by the owner. The approved map pictures remain available in the battlefield picker and manual atlas. New promotional stills, films or page replacements require an owner-directed brief and review; the existence of a capture tool does not authorize replacing the public archive.
docs.guide.studio.1.p2: For a planned shoot, agree on the vehicle, map, time, action and camera progression first. Use the game’s real rigs and effects, capture with the HUD hidden where appropriate, and review motion, framing, exposure and terrain contact before exporting. Preserve reproducible scene settings and distinguish staged material from ordinary gameplay footage.

docs.topic.simulation.roles.t: Bosses, infection, critical damage and weapon ladders
docs.topic.simulation.roles.p1: Juggernaut lets you play the boss or join the hunters. The boss is 12% larger, has a pulsing shield aura, eight times its hull health and half its reload time. Hunters respawn; the boss must survive ten minutes. Infected starts with four infected (at least three in custom battles). Survivors have 30% health; infected have 125%, 40% more speed and faster reloads. Destroyed survivors join the infected. Survive seven minutes, or convert everyone.
docs.topic.simulation.roles.p2: Realistic uses normal spotting and removes hull HP attrition. Penetrations reliably injure crew, apply 2.5× module damage and spread fragments through the struck compartments. Fires damage modules four times faster. Ammunition destruction, fewer than two crew or a destroyed engine and gun eliminate the tank. Gun Game advances through five weapons with two kills per stage; respawns preserve progress.
docs.topic.simulation.flight.t: Direct drone flight and the AC-130 scope
docs.topic.simulation.flight.p1: In Drone mode, press V or tap the drone control to launch a quadcopter from your tank. After the launch animation you directly pilot its first-person view. W/S move, A/D strafe, Space climbs and mouse or touch look steers; pitch down and fly forward to dive. The battery lasts 40 seconds within an 850 m radius. Fly into an enemy to deliver an explosive impact. V returns to your parked, vulnerable tank and starts the 25-second cooldown. National drones have detailed service airframes, camera gimbals and payloads. Large turrets carry the launch rail; compact turrets may use the hull. Impact, battery expiry and manual return trigger a short static transition. The minimap tracks the drone separately from its carrier. I or the sensor button cycles white-hot infrared, colored thermal, green night vision and daylight; the same options are available in tank scopes. Heat highlights visible tanks and bright explosions, without bypassing cover or spotting.
docs.topic.simulation.flight.p2: The AC-130 follows an automatic orbit with an overhead aiming scope. Mouse or touch controls aim; the wheel zooms. Select the 30 mm autocannon, 152 mm explosive howitzer or guided missiles with 1–3 or the ammunition buttons. These have independent reload channels and unlimited ammunition. Shots and drone impacts use the same host-authoritative collision, armor and damage rules as tank weapons. Protect the vulnerable allied ground convoy: escorts have 90% hull strength and must physically reach the green E extraction marker. Save at least half before the eight-minute deadline; losing too many allies fails the mission. The objective tracks surviving troops, rescued troops and route progress. In multiplayer every pilot supplies air support while separate allied bots drive the convoy. Enemies cannot see or shoot the aircraft. Howitzer blasts reach 22 m and missile blasts reach 18 m. J drops ammunition and K drops medical supplies at the ground aim point; icons support touch input. Crates land after six seconds. Nearby allies that need them detour to collect them. Ammo restores finite ground reserves; medicine repairs 35% of maximum health. Cooldowns are 22/30 seconds and crates expire after 70 seconds. The minimap shows the aircraft, orbit, ground aim, extraction and supplies.
